newsitem.title: MEXICO: INTERVIEW - Sidek debt plan set for Nov.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Sidek debt plan set for Nov.

text.p: Mexican conglomerate Grupo Sidek plans to present its debt restructuring plan by the end of November, Director General Luis Rebollar Corona told Reuters in an interview.
Sidek, based in Guadalajara, controls the steel-maker Simec and the tourism business Situr, which was badly hit by the plunging value of its real estate holdings following the 1994 peso crash.
Through the end of September, Grupo Sidek reported a consolidated debt of 16.064 billion pesos, most of it short term and dollar denominated.
"We (at Sidek) are now in agreement on the major announcements that we want to make," Rebollar said. "What we don't have an agreement on yet is how we will reach a consensus (with creditors)."
He said November 30 is the absolute deadline on presenting the plan, adding, "there is no way to extend the period."
Mexican banks extended from June to November the period Sidek had to make its interest and principal payments, giving the company time to restructure its debts.
Analysts said the deal was crucial to Sidek's future.
"They aren't going to be able to pay (their debts)," said Bond Snodgrass of the Abaco brokerage. "It's impossible for them to generate enough cash."
Another U.S.-based analyst said investors would remain uninterested in Sidek ADRs until the restructuring plan were known.
"Everybody is waiting on the restructuring," the analyst said. "The lawsuits are a small problem compared to the others they have."
A U.S. Federal Court this week ordered Sidek to pay about $20 million to its bondholders after three hedge funds sued the company.

Rebollar, who also heads the Situr subsidiary, said Sidek in March proposed auctioning off assets to cover debts, but the plan was rejected by foreign creditors, who hold about 25 percent of the company's debts.
"From the point of view of the company, we are not going to have an auction until well have all of the investors in agreement," Rebollar said.

He said he was confident that Mexican banks would not take any radical steps, saying the grace period was an example of their flexibility. Mexican law allows creditors to seek the dissolution of companies that cannot meet their debts.
"None of them wants to break the company," he said.
